paper.title: Effects of Parental Death on Labor Market Outcomes
paper.code_data_availability: Jensen, Mathias Fjællegaard, and Ning Zhang. 2026. Data and Code for: …

registers.role: treatment: identification of first, sudden parental deaths and their causes
outcomes: labor market participation, earnings, and a proxy for hours worked (ATP payments)
outcomes and controls: sector of employment (public or private), employment
outcomes: number of consultations with private practicing GPs, psychologists, and psychiatrists
outcomes: in- and outpatient hospital visits due to somatic illness; also used to classify the health status of surviving widowed parents
outcomes: hospital visits related to psychiatric treatment
outcomes: medications prescribed by doctors, classified by ATC code (mental health N05*, N06A*, N06B*, N06C*; opioids N02A*; alcohol dependence N07BB*)
outcomes: formal childcare enrollment at the child level (partial coverage in some municipalities, especially before 2005)

registers.name_in_paper: population-level register data from Denmark (Statistics Denmark 2023b)
registers.role: linkage and sample frame: child-parent linkages for children born in the 1950s or later, demographics for the entire population after 1980, cohabitation, region, number of children

linkages: adult children linked to their parents via child-parent linkages available for children born in the 1950s or later
treated individuals linked to matched control individuals by a match ID, which also defines the fixed effects and the clustering level
adult children linked to their spouses for the within-family spillover analysis and to their own children for the formal childcare analysis
adult children linked to the surviving widowed parent's hospitalization records

sample.universe: the full Danish population, 1980-2019, restricted to adult children who experienced their first parental death between 1985 and 2014
sample.unit_of_observation: individual by calendar year (person-year), for event years −5 to +5 around the first parental death, for treated individuals and their matched controls
selection_rules: first parental death occurred between 1985 and 2014 (so that five pre- and five post-event years fall in the 1980-2019 data window)
the first parental death is sudden and unexpected: heart disease, cerebrovascular disease, acute respiratory infections, and traffic or other external accidents
two known parents present in the population the year before the first parental death
aged 25 to 50 years old at the time of the first parental death

for each treated individual, one control individual selected by exact matching on gender, earnings group (four groups, including zero earnings and three quantile categories) and whether the youngest child is above or below six, then nearest-neighbor Mahalanobis matching on age, education level, sector of employment, cohabitation status, residential region, number of children, parental ages, age of the youngest child, and employment and earnings history over the three preceding years
controls must not experience the death of either parent within the five-year window following the treated individual's parental death
sample.period: register data 1980-2019; first parental deaths 1985-2014; health outcomes limited by register start dates (1990 psychologist/GP/psychiatrist, 1994 hospital, 1995 prescriptions and childcare)
sample.n_individuals: 206,286 adult children with a sudden first parental death at t = −1, against 528,057 with a nonsudden first parental death (Table 1)

construction_notes: earnings include income from both employment and self-employment
earnings are winsorized at 98 percent to exclude extreme outliers and are inflation adjusted to 2020 levels using CPI measures from Statistics Denmark (2023a)

for the indexed-earnings outcome, individual earnings are indexed by the average earnings of men and women one year before parental death, so estimates read as percentage changes relative to the baseline mean

labor market participation is measured as strictly positive ATP contributions; the intensive margin is the amount of ATP contributions, which are paid proportionally to hours worked (Kleven, Landais, and Søgaard 2019)
mental-health-related prescriptions are ATC codes N05*, N06A*, N06B* and N06C*; opioid painkillers are N02A*; alcohol dependence treatment is N07BB* (including Antabuse)
hospital visits include both in- and outpatient visits at non-psychiatric hospital wards
in the matching, all variables enter as fixed effects; continuous variables such as earnings are first discretized into quantile groups
for the co-occurrence analysis (Figure 4) the data are restricted to 1995 onward and year −5 is dropped so that the start of treatment can be defined in year −4

surviving widowed parents are classified as ill if they had hospital treatment for more than three months within five years after the first parent's death, including continuous outpatient care (about 20 percent)
proximity to the widowed parent uses NUTS3 regions, dividing Denmark into 11 regions

claims.statement: A sudden first parental death reduces men's employment (participation) by 0.4 percentage points on average over the five years after the death, relative to matched controls.

definition.value: Indicator D_i equal to 1 for individuals whose first parent died suddenly and unexpectedly (heart disease, cerebrovascular disease, acute respiratory infections, and traffic or other external accidents), 0 for their matched controls; interacted with an indicator post_t for observations after the death

timing.value: event year t = 0; outcomes observed from five years before to five years after the first parental death

outcome.label: Employment (labor market participation)

register_source.value: IND/AKM/IDAS/IDAN/IDAP (labor market participation, earnings, proxy for hours worked)

definition.value: Indicator for participation, measured as strictly positive ATP contributions in the year

timing.value: measured annually, five years before to five years after the first parental death

units.value: share (indicator for strictly positive ATP contributions); a coefficient of −0.004 is 0.4 percentage points

estimand.target_population: adult children who experienced a sudden first parental death (effect on the treated, relative to matched controls)
estimand.time_horizon: effects within five years after the first parental death

population.description: Danish adult children aged 25-50 in the year of their first parental death, whose first parent died suddenly between 1985 and 2014 and who had two known parents present in the population the year before, together with their matched controls
population.ages: 25-50 at the time of the first parental death
population.selection: treatment group restricted to sudden, first parental deaths with two known parents; controls selected by exact and nearest-neighbor matching and must not lose a parent within the five-year window

identification.source_of_variation: the timing of sudden, unexpected first parental deaths in 1985-2014, compared with nearest-neighbor matched controls who do not lose a parent within the five-year window

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: the earnings and employment trajectories of individuals who have lost a parent would have otherwise evolved similarly to those of their matched controls following the event
key_assumptions.supported_by: event study estimates from equation (2): raw earnings and employment levels of treated and matched controls are nearly identical before the death (Figure 1); the paper also reports no pre-trend in the mental health outcomes

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: adult children do not anticipate the parental death and adjust their labor market behavior beforehand; the paper addresses this by restricting to sudden and unexpected causes of death
key_assumptions.supported_by: restriction to sudden causes of death (heart disease, cerebrovascular disease, acute respiratory infections, traffic and other external accidents); absence of differential pre-trends in Figure 1

key_assumptions.assumption: No reverse causality: the adult child's own loss of employment and earnings does not cause the parent's death (which would work through reduced family resources worsening the parent's health)
key_assumptions.supported_by: restriction to sudden and unexpected deaths

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional comparability of the matched control: given the matching variables, whether and when an individual's first parent dies suddenly is unrelated to the individual's untreated outcome path
key_assumptions.supported_by: exact matching on gender, earnings group and young-child indicator plus nearest-neighbor Mahalanobis matching on age, education, sector, cohabitation, region, number of children, parental ages, age of youngest child and three years of employment and earnings history; balance shown in Supplemental Appendix Table B.3 panel A

given: employment and earnings history over three years

key_assumptions.assumption: Matched controls are untreated over the window: the control individual does not experience the death of either parent within the five-year window following the treated individual's parental death
key_assumptions.supported_by: construction of the control group in the matching procedure

key_assumptions.assumption: No 'forbidden' comparisons in the staggered design: the design allows only a single, permanent switch from untreated to treated and does not include already treated individuals in the matched controls
key_assumptions.supported_by: footnote 17 discussing the recent staggered-DiD literature (Roth et al. 2023)

threats_discussed: anticipation of the parental death by adult children
reverse causality from the adult child's labor market outcomes to parental health
selection bias from certain groups of parents being more prone to premature death
unobserved and unaccounted-for observed heterogeneity in the descriptive event study without controls
concerns about staggered difference-in-differences designs (Roth et al. 2023)
external validity of sudden relative to nonsudden deaths
robustness_checks: control group of soon-to-be-treated individuals, similar to Fadlon and Nielsen (2021)
adding parents' number of inpatient hospital visits to the matching variables
restricting the treatment group to individuals whose two parental deaths are more than five years apart
restricting the data to 1995 onward and matching on mental health and hospital visit variables
controlling linearly for age and year effects
earnings ranks as an alternative transformation of earnings (Supplemental Appendix Figure B.8)
hospital visits split into screening and nonscreening purposes

timing.value: event year t = 0; outcomes observed from five years before to five years after the first parental death

outcome.label: Start of earnings decline of 5 percent or more

register_source.value: IND/AKM/IDAS/IDAN/IDAP (labor market participation, earnings, proxy for hours worked)

definition.value: Indicator for the onset of a year-to-year earnings decline of at least 5 percent, i.e. a decline not experienced in the previous year. Polarity is given relative to labor market attachment

timing.value: measured annually, five years before to five years after the first parental death

units.value: percentage points (the outcome is a share; its baseline mean is printed as 0.169)

magnitude.interpretation: increases significantly only in the year immediately following parental death

estimand.target_population: adult children who experienced a sudden first parental death (effect on the treated, relative to matched controls)
estimand.time_horizon: the year immediately following parental death

population.description: Danish adult children aged 25-50 in the year of their first parental death, whose first parent died suddenly between 1985 and 2014 and who had two known parents present in the population the year before, together with their matched controls
population.ages: 25-50 at the time of the first parental death
population.selection: treatment group restricted to sudden, first parental deaths with two known parents; controls selected by exact and nearest-neighbor matching and must not lose a parent within the five-year window

identification.source_of_variation: the timing of sudden, unexpected first parental deaths in 1985-2014, compared with nearest-neighbor matched controls who do not lose a parent within the five-year window

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: the earnings and employment trajectories of individuals who have lost a parent would have otherwise evolved similarly to those of their matched controls following the event
key_assumptions.supported_by: event study estimates from equation (2): raw earnings and employment levels of treated and matched controls are nearly identical before the death (Figure 1); the paper also reports no pre-trend in the mental health outcomes

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: adult children do not anticipate the parental death and adjust their labor market behavior beforehand; the paper addresses this by restricting to sudden and unexpected causes of death
key_assumptions.supported_by: restriction to sudden causes of death (heart disease, cerebrovascular disease, acute respiratory infections, traffic and other external accidents); absence of differential pre-trends in Figure 1

key_assumptions.assumption: No reverse causality: the adult child's own loss of employment and earnings does not cause the parent's death (which would work through reduced family resources worsening the parent's health)
key_assumptions.supported_by: restriction to sudden and unexpected deaths

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional comparability of the matched control: given the matching variables, whether and when an individual's first parent dies suddenly is unrelated to the individual's untreated outcome path
key_assumptions.supported_by: exact matching on gender, earnings group and young-child indicator plus nearest-neighbor Mahalanobis matching on age, education, sector, cohabitation, region, number of children, parental ages, age of youngest child and three years of employment and earnings history; balance shown in Supplemental Appendix Table B.3 panel A

given: employment and earnings history over three years

key_assumptions.assumption: Matched controls are untreated over the window: the control individual does not experience the death of either parent within the five-year window following the treated individual's parental death
key_assumptions.supported_by: construction of the control group in the matching procedure

key_assumptions.assumption: No 'forbidden' comparisons in the staggered design: the design allows only a single, permanent switch from untreated to treated and does not include already treated individuals in the matched controls
key_assumptions.supported_by: footnote 17 discussing the recent staggered-DiD literature (Roth et al. 2023)

threats_discussed: anticipation of the parental death by adult children
reverse causality from the adult child's labor market outcomes to parental health
selection bias from certain groups of parents being more prone to premature death
unobserved and unaccounted-for observed heterogeneity in the descriptive event study without controls
concerns about staggered difference-in-differences designs (Roth et al. 2023)
external validity of sudden relative to nonsudden deaths
robustness_checks: control group of soon-to-be-treated individuals, similar to Fadlon and Nielsen (2021)
adding parents' number of inpatient hospital visits to the matching variables
restricting the treatment group to individuals whose two parental deaths are more than five years apart
restricting the data to 1995 onward and matching on mental health and hospital visit variables
controlling linearly for age and year effects
earnings ranks as an alternative transformation of earnings (Supplemental Appendix Figure B.8)
hospital visits split into screening and nonscreening purposes

estimator.value: OLS on matched treated-control panel with individual, year, time-since-event and age fixed effects (two-way fixed effects DiD)

estimation.specification: This is one of the co-occurrence outcomes the paper uses instead of a mediation analysis, because health measures affected by parental death would be 'bad controls'.

source_table.value: Figure 4, panel B (event-time coefficient in the year after the death, stated in the text)

adjustment_set.label: individual by match ID fixed effects

population.selection: treatment group restricted to sudden, first parental deaths with two known parents; controls selected by exact and nearest-neighbor matching and must not lose a parent within the five-year window

identification.source_of_variation: variation in age at the time of the first parental death, with age-by-year and education-by-year controls; no control group

key_assumptions.assumption: The event-time coefficients are identified from variation in age at the time of the first parental death, with age-by-year and education-by-year controls; no control group is used
key_assumptions.supported_by: footnote 13 setting out equation (1) and its controls

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: adult children do not adjust behavior before the death; addressed by restricting to sudden and unexpected causes of death
key_assumptions.supported_by: restriction to sudden causes of death

threats_discussed: anticipation of the parental death by adult children
reverse causality from the adult child's labor market outcomes to parental health
selection bias from certain groups of parents being more prone to premature death
unobserved and unaccounted-for observed heterogeneity in the descriptive event study without controls
concerns about staggered difference-in-differences designs (Roth et al. 2023)
external validity of sudden relative to nonsudden deaths
robustness_checks: control group of soon-to-be-treated individuals, similar to Fadlon and Nielsen (2021)
adding parents' number of inpatient hospital visits to the matching variables
restricting the treatment group to individuals whose two parental deaths are more than five years apart
restricting the data to 1995 onward and matching on mental health and hospital visit variables
controlling linearly for age and year effects
earnings ranks as an alternative transformation of earnings (Supplemental Appendix Figure B.8)
hospital visits split into screening and nonscreening purposes
unresolved_confounders: both unobserved and unaccounted-for observed heterogeneity may drive general trends and gender differences in outcomes (the paper's own stated limitation of this descriptive exercise)

estimator.value: OLS event-study regression on the treatment group only (equation 1)

estimation.specification: equation (1), estimated separately for women and men
fixed_effects: age in year dummies interacted with year fixed effects
education-level fixed effects interacted with year fixed effects

source_table.value: Supplemental Appendix Figure B.5, panel D (described in the text)

adjustment_set.label: age in year dummies interacted with year fixed effects
education-level fixed effects interacted with year fixed effects

nodes: Any prescriptions related to mental health

edges.to: Any prescriptions related to mental health
given: individual by match ID fixed effects

value.as_printed: Y_ity = Σ_{k=−5, k≠−1}^{5} δ_k · 1[k = t] + Age Year_iy + Edu Year_iy + ε_ity

index_sets.over: individuals (treated adult children and their matched controls)
calendar years
years from the first parental death, −5 to 5

value.normalisation: the year before the event (k = −1) is omitted and serves as the reference year

target_designation.reasoning: The descriptive event-study equation designates δ_k as the coefficients of interest.

basis.reasoning: The descriptive 15 percent rise in men's prescriptions is from the uncontrolled descriptive analysis rather than the cited matched-control result.
